notes.meaning: David asked if anyone was still alive from King Saul's family so he could show them favor. Saul had been David's enemy, but Jonathan was his closest friend, and the two had made a covenant—a sacred promise before God—to protect each other's families. While new kings in that world usually wiped out rival royal houses, David actively searched for a chance to keep his word and do good.

David's court found a man named Ziba, who had been a trusted servant managing Saul's household. When brought before the king, David asked him directly to confirm who he was. Ziba answered with deep respect, presenting himself ready to serve the king.

David asked Ziba if anyone remained of Saul's family so he could show them the "kindness of God." This meant a very great mercy, copying the generous love that God shows to people. Ziba reported that Jonathan had a surviving son who could not walk on either foot.

David asked where this son could be found. Ziba explained that he was living east of the Jordan River in Lo-debar, staying in the home of a wealthy supporter named Machir. Jonathan's son owned no property of his own and was living quietly out of sight.

King David sent messengers to Lo-debar to bring Jonathan's son to the royal capital. David did not expect a man with crippled feet to travel alone, so he provided safe transport. Machir had sheltered the young prince out of pure kindness, and David now took over his care.

Jonathan's son, Mephibosheth, arrived and bowed facedown to the floor before David. Coming from a fallen dynasty, he likely feared he might be put to death. David warmly greeted him by name, and Mephibosheth answered with humble obedience.

David told Mephibosheth not to be afraid, promising to treat him with faithful kindness for Jonathan's sake. He gave back all the family land that had belonged to his grandfather Saul. Even greater, David offered him a permanent seat at the royal table as an honored guest.

Mephibosheth bowed again, amazed by such generous mercy. He called himself a "dead dog," an ancient expression for someone completely worthless and helpless. He did not treat David's gifts as something owed to him, but received them with deep gratitude.

David called Ziba into the room to announce the legal decision. The king had restored all of Saul's former private estate to Saul's grandson Mephibosheth. This royal decree made Mephibosheth a wealthy landowner overnight.

David ordered Ziba, his fifteen sons, and his twenty servants to farm the land and bring in the crops for Mephibosheth. The harvest would supply food and income for Mephibosheth's household and staff. Meanwhile, Mephibosheth himself would always dine at the king's royal table.

Ziba promised to obey every order the king had given. From that time on, Mephibosheth ate his meals at David's table like one of the king's own sons. He was welcomed into the intimate circle and honor of the royal family.

Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica, through whom Jonathan's family line would continue for future generations. All the members of Ziba's household became workers who farmed the land for Mephibosheth. In this way, God preserved the house of Jonathan in safety and honor.

Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem so he could eat daily at the king's table, even though he was lame in both feet. David's favor did not remove his physical weakness, but it completely changed his standing and life. He lived in close fellowship with the king who loved him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars suggest David may have had political motives, keeping Mephibosheth close in Jerusalem partly to watch over the last potential rival from Saul's royal line.
